items.summary: Two unowned product decisions, not drift: (a) whether a band's EPK may foreground credits its members hold personally, and with whose consent; (b) whether a human-scoped EPK discloses the sender's privately-linked aliases to the named recipient. Both change what the product does for a user and neither has an answer anywhere in the tree. NOT fixed. items.ownerBrief:
TWO DECISIONS ON THE EPK, BOTH BLOCKING AN IMPLEMENTER.

(1) MAY A BAND'S EPK FOREGROUND ITS MEMBERS' PERSONAL CREDITS?
Settled already: who may SEND a band's EPK (a mandate, 01.03.03). Never settled: what it may CONTAIN. A band holds its own credits, but "our drummer played on {famous record}" is the strongest line in a support-slot pitch and that credit is the drummer's, not the band's. The tree bars the opposite direction explicitly — no roll-up from a band credit into a member's portfolio (02.01.02 D-14) — and is silent on this one, which is not the same as permitting it.
  Option A — band-held credits only. Safe, consistent with the no-roll-up rule, and throws away the pitch's best material. Costs the platform its own advantage at the moment the EPK exists to win.
  Option B — member credits with per-member consent at generation. Honest, and matches the consent posture used everywhere else in this domain. Cost: 01.06.03 D-02 makes EPKs per-pitch and therefore frequent, so this adds a consent round-trip to a routine action, and a member who is slow to answer silently weakens a live pitch.
  Option C — member credits by default, on the ground that they are already public on the member's own page. Fastest and what users will expect. But it lets a band pitch on the strength of a member who has since left — the legacy-act deception 01.01.02 DT-05 refuses when the same thing happens through an alias transfer, arriving here through a surface that rule does not cover.
  RECOMMENDATION: B, with the consent held per member rather than per send (grant once, revocable), so the friction is paid once instead of every pitch. Option C's departed-member case is the one that produces a promoter who was misled, which is the harm class this platform sells the cure for.

(2) DOES A HUMAN-SCOPED EPK DISCLOSE THE SENDER'S PRIVATELY-LINKED ALIASES?
01.06.02 D-07 computes the human portfolio over publicly-linked aliases only and forbids any derived fact varying observably — but it scopes that invariant to the PUBLIC portfolio. An EPK is a disclosure to one named recipient, not a publication, so the invariant does not reach it, and 01.06.02's own cross-cut note calls this unmodelled.
  The case that makes it real: a producer pitching a mix service WANTS this one booker to see three names' worth of career, and spent that career keeping those names apart in public (01.01.02 D-07 exists for exactly that person).
  Option A — fail closed. The EPK inherits the public visible set; including a privately-linked alias is a deliberate per-send opt-in with a disclosure line. Consistent with the tree's standing fail-closed posture (01.01.02 D-07, 01.01.04 DT-01). Cost: friction on the pitch that most needs the full career.
  Option B — sender's choice, no gate. The kit is theirs to compose and they chose the recipient. Cost, and it is not small: 01.06.03 D-06 makes the link a forwardable tracking wrapper over public content with no access gate, so a one-tap include lands in a room the sender never picked, permanently, and linkage is reversible while disclosure is not.
  RECOMMENDATION: A. The asymmetry decides it — a wrong include cannot be taken back, and D-06 guarantees the forward.

BOTH ARE ROUTED: Q-04 to /create-prd, Q-05 to /create-prd-security (matching 01.06.03 Q-03's routing for the adjacent link-expiry question).
